data.title: The navy of ancient Greece – penteconters, triremes and sea power
data.excerpt: The navy of ancient Greece was one of the most important military and merchant navies of the ancient world, and the Athenians above all were renowned for their seamanship and their warships. From the fifty-oared penteconter to the trireme with its three banks of oars, this article follows the ships themselves, the way the fleets were funded and manned, the navies of Athens, Sparta, Phoenicia and Corinth, and the wreck of the Kyrenia ship.
data.metaTitle: The navy of ancient Greece: penteconters and triremes
data.metaDescription: Penteconters, triremes and the Kyrenia wreck. How the ships, crews and funding of the ancient Greek navy shaped warfare and trade in the Mediterranean.

children.text: Introduction

The navy of ancient Greece was one of the most important military and merchant navies of the ancient world. The Greeks, and the Athenians in particular, were renowned for their seamanship and their warships. The navy had a considerable influence on Greek culture and art. Sea battles, warships and the sea itself were frequent themes in Greek literature and art. The navy of ancient Greece played an important role in history and shaped the development of naval warfare and of trade throughout the Mediterranean.
1. The navy of ancient Greece

Among the earliest written mentions we may count the descriptions of Greek ships in the works of ancient writers. Authors of books devoted to this subject in the territory of present-day Slovakia include J. KOPECKY. His book „O lodích Rěků a Řimanů“ (On the Ships of the Greeks and the Romans) was published in Prague in 1886. The ancient Greek navy was one of the most important components of Greek culture and society. The Greeks were outstanding seafarers, and their fleets allowed them to colonise a large part of the Mediterranean, to trade with other countries and to win wars.

The Greeks founded colonies all over the Mediterranean. Ships were indispensable for transporting people, supplies and livestock to these new territories. The Greek colonies were important for the Greek economy and culture. The ancient Greek navy had a great influence on the development of seafaring in Europe. Its design features and tactics remained in use right up to the Middle Ages.

At the beginning of the Archaic period there were a number of smaller fleets of local character. Ownership of such ships was at first private. In times of war all the ships officially came under the single command of the leading representatives of the individual communities, but in peacetime their activity was independent of them and they followed solely the orders of their owner, often with the aim of enriching their owners and crews personally. The crews were mostly made up of volunteers seeking personal gain. Armament was provided either by each man at his own expense, or by the owner of the ship.

The Greeks had been able traders since time immemorial. Ships allowed them to trade with other parts of the Mediterranean and the Near East. They traded in various commodities, including wine, olive oil, pottery and luxury goods.
1.2. Ships

The Greeks used various types of ship, including merchant ships, warships and sporting ships. Greek merchant ships and warships were often smaller and more manoeuvrable than the ships of other seafaring peoples, which allowed them to put in even at small harbours. They were built of wood and had one or two banks of oars, and one or more masts. On deck they had a cargo space in which goods were carried.

Sporting ships were used for races and for various contests, such as the Olympic Games. They were similar to merchant ships, but lighter and faster. They were made of wood and had oars. The ships of the 8th century BC described by Homer are referred to as „swift and hollow“. The size of the ships varied. Boats for short journeys and merchant vessels had twenty oars, and the largest ship of that time was the penteconter, which had fifty oars. It was a long, narrow vessel used both as a warship and as a transport vessel.

An important type of ship in ancient Greece was the trireme, which had three banks of oars. Triremes were fast and manoeuvrable and were armed with a ram, with which they could damage or sink enemy ships. Warships were larger and stronger than merchant ships. They were built of wood and had one or more banks of oars.

Another interesting type of vessel was undoubtedly the monoxylon, which may be counted among the vessels used perhaps most frequently and for the longest time of all, precisely because of how it was built and how readily available it was.
1.2.1 The penteconter

The penteconter was an ancient Greek ship in use from the Archaic period onwards. Penteconters appeared at a time when there was no distinction between merchant ships and warships. They were all-purpose ships capable of sailing great distances, which made them useful for maritime trade, piracy and warfare, able to carry cargo or military units. The hull was black, the forward part was usually painted red or blue and decorated with a figurehead. The stern of the ship was raised. Both the bow and the stern ended in horns like those of a cow, or curled like a ram’s horns. Fifty oarsmen rowed in a single row of twenty-five on each side of the ship. In a favourable wind the ship could also be driven by a central mast with a sail. Penteconters were long ships with a sharp keel, and were therefore described as long vessels (νῆες μακραί, nḗes makraí). They usually lacked a full deck, and so were also called unfenced vessels (ἄφρακτοι νῆες, áphraktoi nḗes).

Homer describes warships during the Trojan War with varying numbers of oars, from twenty-oared ones – such as the ship that brought Chryseis back to her father – to fifty-oared ones, such as Odysseus’ ship, which had fifty-seven men, and up to 120 men on raiders’ ships. According to some present-day calculations it is assumed that penteconters were between 28 and 33 m (92 and 108 feet) long, about 4 m wide and capable of reaching a maximum speed of 9 knots (17 km/h; 10 mph). However, modern reconstructions of penteconters, as well as of other ancient ship designs such as triremes, crewed by untrained modern amateurs, reached this top speed fairly easily during the initial sea trials, which means that the maximum speed of this type of ship in antiquity must have been considerably higher. The ancient Greeks also used the triakonter or triakontor (τριακόντορος triakontoros), a shorter version of the penteconter with thirty oars. There is general agreement that the trireme, the principal warship of classical antiquity, developed from the penteconter by way of the bireme. The penteconter remained in use until the Hellenistic period, when it was supplemented and finally replaced by other designs, such as the lembus, the hemiolia and the liburnians.
1.2.2 The dieres

The dieres is an ancient oared warship (a galley) with two banks of oars placed one above the other on each side. Diereis were long vessels built for military purposes and could reach a relatively high speed. They were invented long before the 6th century BC and were used by the Phoenicians, the Assyrians and the Greeks. The Romans called this type of ship a bireme. The name bireme comes from „bi“, meaning two, and „remus“, meaning oar. The typical dimensions of a dieres were about 80 feet (24 m) in length with a maximum width of about 10 feet (3 m). It is assumed that it developed from the penteconter, a ship which had only one set of oars on each side, whereas the bireme had two sets of oars on each side. The dieres was twice the length and height of the triakonter, and therefore employed 120 oarsmen. The diereis included galleys, galleasses, dromons and small pleasure vessels called pamphyloi. The further development of this type of vessel gave rise to the trireme, to which, while the length of the bireme was retained, a further deck was added, raising the number of oarsmen to 180. It also had a large square sail.
1.2.3 The trireme

The trireme is a type of Greek warship developed at the turn of the 4th and 5th centuries BC. The ships had one or two masts with a rectangular sail, which served as an additional means of propulsion, and oarsmen in three banks one above the other. The Romans called these ships triremes. The large number of oars gave them great speed and manoeuvrability. On deck they were fitted with fighting towers, from which arrows were shot and stones hurled. The trireme was built of wood, usually of oak or pine. It had a horseshoe-shaped hull, which was designed to be stable while rowing. The trireme was armed with 20 to 30 bronze rams. The rams were placed at the front of the ship and were used to breach the hull of an enemy ship. The ship also carried a number of archers and spearmen. The trireme was used for fighting on the open sea. It was highly manoeuvrable and could change direction quickly. This allowed it to manoeuvre around enemy ships and attack them from the side. Triremes were also used to transport soldiers and supplies to the theatre of war. The trireme was of fundamental importance to ancient Greek civilisation. It was the key to the success of the Greek naval campaigns and helped the Greeks to extend their power and influence throughout the Mediterranean.
Dimensions of the trireme:
length – 35 m
width – 6 m
height – 3 m
crew: approximately 200 men, of whom 170 were oarsmen + the remaining components (10 hoplites + 4 archers + officers and command staff)
characteristic qualities of the trireme: speed and mobility. In a single day it could cover up to 240 km.
1.2.4 The monoxylon

Monoxyla were also used in ancient Greece. These were small, single-oarsman boats made from a single piece of wood. Poplar wood, for example, was often used to build this type of vessel. Monoxyla were already known in the Minoan civilisation, which developed on Crete in the 2nd and 3rd millennia BC. In Greek mythology monoxyla are mentioned in the myths of Odysseus and Jason. Fishing – monoxyla were popular boats for fishing. They were light and manoeuvrable, which allowed fishermen to approach the fish easily.
Transport of people and goods
– monoxyla were also used to transport people and goods. They were used to carry people between harbours and to carry goods over short distances.
Military purposes

– monoxyla were also used for military purposes. They were used to transport soldiers and supplies to the theatre of war. Monoxyla were an important part of Greek civilisation. They were used for a variety of purposes and helped the Greeks to develop trade, colonisation and military power. Some of the significant kinds of monoxyla in ancient Greece include:
Kybelos, which was used to transport people and goods on Crete.
Kouris, which was used for fishing and for carrying people on the Greek peninsula.
Pentera, which was used for military purposes.
Kybelos

was a type of Greek monoxylon boat used to transport people and goods on Crete in the Minoan and Mycenaean civilisations (c. 3000–1100 BC). Kybeloi were relatively large monoxyla, up to 15 metres long and up to 3 metres wide. They were driven by 20–30 oarsmen, who sat on one side of the boat. Kybeloi also had a sail, which was used as an additional means of propulsion. Kybeloi were used for a variety of purposes, including:- Trade: kybeloi were used to carry goods between Crete and other islands and countries in the Mediterranean Sea. - Colonisation: kybeloi were used to carry people and supplies to the new territories that the Cretans were colonising.
- Military purposes: kybeloi were also used for military purposes, for example to transport soldiers and supplies to the theatre of war.
Some of the evidence for kybeloi includes:
Frescoes from the Minoan palace at Knossos that depict kybeloi.
Terracotta models of kybeloi found in Minoan and Mycenaean tombs.
The wreck of a kybelos found off the coast of Crete.
Kouris

was a type of Greek monoxylon boat used for fishing and for carrying people on the Greek peninsula in Archaic and Classical Greece (c. 800–323 BC). Kourides were popular boats for fishing. They were light and manoeuvrable, which allowed fishermen to approach the fish easily. Kourides were also used to carry people over short distances. Terracotta models of kourides have been found in Greek tombs.

Kybeloi and kourides were both types of monoxylon boat, but there were some key differences between them. Kybeloi were larger and driven by a greater number of oarsmen, whereas kourides were smaller and driven by a single oarsman. Kybeloi also had a sail, whereas kourides did not always have one.
1.3. Organisation and funding of the navy

In the earliest times ships and vessels were in private ownership. At the end of the 6th century a change came about in the funding of the navy in Greece. Three factors in particular contributed to this. The first was the effort to adapt to, and keep pace with, the leading maritime communities in Asia Minor. The second factor was the response to the growing influence and pressure of the Persian Empire. Positions of power were being created in the Aegean and control was being taken of the trade and trade routes there). Competition and mutual rivalry between some of the communities (for example Athens and Aegina) was the third reason for the change in the ownership of the fleets. The character of the funding of shipbuilding changed. Instead of the private resources of wealthy owners, money from public funds began to be used.

Building up a naval fleet became a chief priority for many cities. From what had until then been purely private ownership, the ownership of ships became public, and an enterprise directly supported and financed by the state came into being. Among the first communities to possess a „larger“ number of triremes were, for example, Corinth, Athens, Aegina, Eretria and Corcyra.) In order to secure the money needed for the running of a fleet it was also necessary to secure the required number of men for the crews. About 200 men served in the crew of a single trireme, which caused considerable problems, especially for the smaller communities. In the larger cities – the poleis – special funds were set up for financing, along with a number of new central offices which supervised both the building and the technical provisioning of the ships and the securing of the required number of men for their crews.
2. The best-known and most successful Greek navies
The Greek navy was one of the most powerful in the ancient world. The Greeks used ships to attack enemy cities and to defend their own. Greek ships were also important for battles at sea.
The Athenian navy in the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BC)
The Spartan navy in the Peloponnesian War
The Phoenician navy in the 6th century BC
The Corinthian navy in the 5th century BC
2.1. The Athenian navy

The Athenian navy was a key factor in the success of Athens in the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BC). The Athenians were a naval power, and their navy allowed them to control the Mediterranean Sea and to isolate Sparta from its allies. The Athenian navy was based on the system of the Athenian naval league. This league comprised about 300 Greek cities, which paid tribute to Athens. These payments were used to finance the Athenian navy.

The Athenian navy was under the command of the Athenian strategoi, who were elected each year. The strategoi were responsible for planning and conducting naval operations. These victories helped Athens to maintain its power and to prevent Sparta from conquering the Athenian empire. The administration of the navy in Athens was carried out at the level of territorial administration. There were units known as naukraries (naukrariai) – territorial and administrative districts. At their head stood the naukraroi (ship captains). The task of the captains was to designate each year, from among the wealthiest citizens of the given naukrary, those who were to finance the building of a certain number of ships out of their own resources – 1 citizen = 1 ship. Command of the fleet at the „national“ level lay with the polemarchos (de iure); de facto it lay with the individual captains (that is, the owners of the ships), who, thanks to financing the construction of the ships and caring for them all year round, gained a number of advantages, above all of a political nature (for example holding high state offices). The community took practically no part at all in financing the building of a ship. The crews were seen to separately in each naukrary, and the captains were responsible for them. The other communities (for example Samos, Corinth, Eretria, Corcyra and Chalcis) had the same manner of financing construction and of organisation, based on private ownership of the ships. The drawbacks of this manner of financing were:
1.) the lack of state involvement in financing construction – the state had no direct control over the use of the ships, and so they were often used by their owners for their own personal enrichment.

2.) the fleets of the individual maritime communities were small as a result of the demands of, and the manner of, their financing and material provisioning (for example Athens 50, Alalia 60, Samos 100 ships). In the 490s BC Athens acquired its first triremes by purchasing them from Corinth with the public funds of the city-state. In 483 the naval programme for building up the navy, associated with Themistocles, began to operate. The reason for its creation was the war with Aegina (an island not far from Attica, a traditional competitor and enemy of Athens). Money was provided from public funds (the revenues from the silver mines at Laurion) to the 100 wealthiest citizens for the building of ships – each citizen had one ship in his charge and upkeep. Gradually the naval programme became the chief priority in Athens. Money was provided from public resources for the building of the fleet. Its material provisioning and organisation came directly under the supervision of the executive body of the community – the Council of Five Hundred (the boule). Alongside the financing of construction, the greatest problem for the community was securing a sufficient number of men for the ships’ crews; as the number of ships grew (about 200 in the year 480), they therefore had to call up not only their own citizens but also foreigners (metics) and slaves for the crews, or else hire mercenaries.
Composition of the crews and the hierarchy of command:
1. nauarchos (admiral) – stood at the head of the whole fleet; all the trierarchs were subordinate to him, and he was mostly chosen from among the strategoi then in office

2.) trierarchos – a formal title rather than a military function; chiefly responsible for the pay and the provisioning of the crew; often he was not even personally present on the ship and delegated his authority to one of the members of the crew. 3.) epibatai – volunteer soldiers from the ranks of the citizens, serving as the guard of the ship – as a rule 10 hoplites + 4 archers (toxotai); they belonged to the so-called working-class hoplites. Service in the fleet was not regarded as military service in the true sense of the word – the obligation of general mobilisation did not apply to it. They alone were able to take part, together with the captain, in military councils and political deliberations.

4.) hyperesia – the ship’s crew – at its head stood the kybernetes, the helmsman and navigator, the most experienced member of the crew; in the captain’s absence he stood in for him and commanded the ship.
The other members of the crew were:
o proirates – the lookout
o keleustes – the commander of the oarsmen
o naupegos – the shipwright – he was in charge of repairs to damaged parts of the ship
o pentekontarchos – the purser – he saw to the payment of wages and the provisioning of the crew
o about 10 further assistants
5.) the oarsmen – 170 men divided, rising upwards, into 3 banks on both sides of the ship.
the upper bank – thranitai – 62 – the most experienced and socially the highest placed (Athenian citizens)
the middle bank – zygioi – 54 – chiefly foreigners and less experienced citizens

the lower bank – thalamoi – 54 – the lowest social standing of all – chiefly slaves, or foreigners with the least experience. Rowing was purely a matter for the lowest social strata – the propertied were exempt from this service even in the event of acute danger.
The most important victories of the Athenians were:

the battle of Salamis (480 BC). The battle of Salamis was a naval battle between the Greek city-states and Persia which took place in September 480 BC between Piraeus and the island state of Salamis, a small island in the Gulf of Aegina near Athens.
the battle of Mycale (479 BC). The battle of Mycale was the last significant battle of the Greco-Persian Wars. It took place on the same day as the battle of Plataea.
the battle of Arginusae (406 BC). This defeat led to the defeat of Athens in the Peloponnesian War and to the end of Athenian naval supremacy.

The Athenian navy was a key factor in the success of Athens in the Peloponnesian War. The Athenians were a naval power, and their navy allowed them to control the Mediterranean Sea and to isolate Sparta from its allies.
The Athenian navy was used for the following purposes:
Protecting the Athenian merchant fleet
The frontiers of the Athenian empire
Attacking enemy territory
Transporting soldiers and supplies
2.2. The Spartan navy

The Spartan navy was a secondary factor in the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BC). Sparta was a land power and its navy was smaller and less experienced than the Athenian navy, yet it was an important factor in several battles during the war. Sparta’s victories at Cyzicus and Arginusae helped the Spartans to gain control of the Aegean Sea and to isolate Athens from its allies. The Spartan navy was based on the system of the community. Every community had the duty to provide a certain number of oarsmen and ships. The Spartan navy was under the command of the Spartan kings. The kings were responsible for planning and conducting naval operations. So was the Spartan navy weak? It depends which period we are asking about. In general, Sparta was not a significant naval power. There was, however, one decade during which the Spartans had – temporarily – the most powerful fleet in Greece.

The Peloponnesian War (or wars) lasted a whole generation, from 431 to 404 BC. For most of that time the Spartan navy was at best negligible: the Spartans generally conceded the sea to the Athenians, while the Athenians largely refused to face the Spartan army on land. As late as 413 the Spartan fleet consisted of only a few dozen vessels, while the Athenians put to sea fleets as large as four hundred. In the last decade of the war, however, the Spartans concluded an alliance with Persia. The Persians financed the creation and training of a new, larger fleet. Persian gold paid for the ships, but, more importantly, it paid for the oarsmen – no Spartan warrior would demean himself by pulling an oar, but slave oarsmen repeatedly proved inferior in motivation and skill to the free citizens who drove the Athenian fleet.

With this money the Spartans were able to recruit mercenary oarsmen from all over the eastern Mediterranean, especially from the Greek cities in Persian territory and from Phoenicia. Not a few of them were hired directly or indirectly from the Athenians themselves:

The most important victories of the Spartans were the battle of Cyzicus (410 BC) and the battle of Arginusae (406 BC). In the end, however, the Spartan navy was defeated at the battle of Aegospotami (405 BC). This defeat led to the defeat of Sparta in the Peloponnesian War and to the end of Athenian naval supremacy.
The Athenian and the Spartan navy differed from each other in the following respects:
Basis
: the Athenian navy was based on the system of the Athenian naval league, whereas the Spartan navy was based on the system of the community.
Size
: the Athenian navy was larger and stronger than the Spartan navy.
Experience
: the Athenian navy was more experienced than the Spartan navy.
Armament
: the Athenian navy was better armed than the Spartan navy.

The Athenian and the Spartan navy were important factors in the Peloponnesian War. The Athenian navy was a key factor in the success of Athens in the first phase of the war, while the Spartan navy played an important role in the later phase of the war.

children.text: 2.3. The Phoenician navy

The Phoenician navy in the 6th century BC was one of the most powerful naval forces in the Mediterranean. The Phoenicians were traders and seafarers, and their navy was an important instrument of their economic and political influence. The Phoenicians became seafarers above all because of the geographical conditions in which they lived. Travel between the cities, which usually lay on rocky peninsulas, was far easier by sea than by land. Especially when they were carrying heavy cargo, such as cedar logs, a typical Phoenician trade commodity. One of the Phoenician cities was Tyre, which lay on an island, so that ships were the most practical means of transport for its inhabitants. For this people, surrounded by mountains, the natural expansion was therefore not inland, but towards the sea. As a result of the search for new resources, such as gold and tin, the Phoenicians began to develop their seafaring skills rapidly from about the 12th century BC. They created an extensive trade network which stretched from Cyprus, through Rhodes, the islands of the Aegean Sea, Egypt, Sicily, Malta, Sardinia, central Italy, France, North Africa, Ibiza and Spain, as far as beyond the Pillars of Hercules (in antiquity the name for the area of the Strait of Gibraltar). This trade network was gradually transformed into a Phoenician empire of colonies.
The Phoenician navy was made up of various types of ship, including penteres, triremes and dromons. The Phoenicians used their navy for the following purposes:
Trade: the Phoenicians used their navy to carry goods from all over the Mediterranean.
Colonisation: the Phoenicians used their navy to settle new territories in the Mediterranean.
Expeditions: the Phoenicians used their navy for expeditions against neighbouring cities and countries.

The Phoenician navy was successful in many battles and naval expeditions. The most important victories of the Phoenicians were the battle of Lade (664 BC) and the battle of Mycale (479 BC). In the end, however, the Phoenician navy was destroyed in 546 BC, when the Phoenicians were defeated by Lydia.
Examples of Phoenician naval expeditions in the 6th century BC:

664 BC: the Phoenicians defeated the Lydian fleet at the battle of Lade. This battle marked the end of Lydian supremacy in the Aegean Sea. Lydia (Gr. Λυδία) was an ancient state in the west of Asia Minor. It was inhabited by the Lydians (Gr. Λυδοί – Lydi), a people of Indo-European origin who used the Greek alphabet.
650 BC: the Phoenicians founded the colony of Massilia (present-day Marseille) on the coast of France.
630 BC: the Phoenicians founded the colony of Phocaea (present-day Foça) in Turkey.
546 BC: the Phoenician navy was defeated by Lydia. This defeat marked the end of Phoenician naval supremacy.
2.4. The Corinthian navy

The Corinthian navy in the 5th century BC was one of the most powerful naval forces in Greece. The Corinthians were traders and seafarers, and their navy was an important instrument of their economic and political influence. The Corinthians used their navy for the following purposes:
Trade: the Corinthians used their navy to carry goods from all over the Mediterranean.
Colonisation: the Corinthians used their navy to settle new territories in the Mediterranean.
Expeditions: the Corinthians used their navy for expeditions against neighbouring cities and countries.
The Corinthian navy was successful in many battles and naval expeditions. The most important victories of the Corinthians were the battle of Salamis (480 BC) and the battle of Potidaea (432 BC).

In the end, however, the Corinthian navy was defeated by Athens in the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BC). The Corinthian navy was an important factor in the rise of Corinth as a naval and trading power. The Corinthians used their navy to extend their trade and to colonise new territories. The Corinthian navy also played an important role in the Greco-Persian Wars.
3. A remarkable archaeological find of a historic ship

In the winter of 1967 the Greek Cypriot diver Andreas Kariolou chanced upon traces of a unique monument of antiquity in the depths of the sea off the town of Kyrenia – a ship later known as the „Kyrenia ship“. It was subsequently excavated by Michael Katzev of the American Institute of Nautical Archaeology. The Kyrenia ship was built at the beginning of the 4th century BC and is the oldest Greek vessel ever discovered. Ancient shipwrecks have been found elsewhere in the Mediterranean Sea, and the few parts of them that have been studied have yielded valuable, but as yet incomplete, information about the methods used in building ancient ships. In this context the significance of the Kyrenia ship is considerable, since it is the best-preserved ship of the classical period of Greek civilisation ever found. It is important to note that 75% of the ship, which was 15 metres long, has survived, because it was protected beneath a protective layer of sand. Among the cargo recovered were amphorae used for transporting wine and for storing almonds. The Greek merchant ship carried a cargo of up to 500 amphorae, which belonged to ten different shape types. Most of the amphorae originated on Rhodes and were dated to the last third of the 4th century BC. This ship, probably a merchantman, carried various goods such as tableware and cutlery, tools, ship’s equipment and even four bone eyelets from sailors’ sandals. The site of the shipwreck extended over an area of about nineteen metres in length and ten metres in width. One remarkable feature was 27 millstones stacked in three rows along the axis of the ship to serve as ballast. During the investigation small fragments of thin lead sheeting with bronze tacks were also found, and later larger sheets were uncovered as well, which indicates that the Greek ship was covered with a lead sheathing that protected its hull. A large part of the hull had survived. The remains of the ship’s hull that were found were raised from the sea, conserved and reconstructed. The reconstructed hull was 14 m long and 4.2 m wide. Conservation of the wreck took place between 1969 and 1974.
5. Conclusion

Ships and the navy were an important part of Greek civilisation. They were used for a variety of purposes and helped the Greeks to develop trade, colonisation and military power. This fact shaped culture, trade and practically every aspect of life for centuries to come.
Author: Veronika Beranová
